<description>
{
 "summary": "Enables SQLite's `secure_delete` PRAGMA by default on all wallet database connections and sets `-DSQLITE_SECURE_DELETE` in the SQLite depends package. Deleted or updated database records are overwritten with zeroes instead of remaining in unallocated SQLite database pages. Removes the `WalletDatabase::Rewrite` interface (which previously invoked `VACUUM` only upon initial encryption) and adds functional tests for plaintext and rotated key erasure.",
 "problem": "Modifications and deletions in SQLite wallet files leave data in unallocated database pages. Initial encryption previously avoided leaving unencrypted keys in slack space by running an explicit `VACUUM` rewrite, but other sensitive operations\u2014such as rotating master encryption keys during passphrase changes\u2014left obsolete key records visible in database free space.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: 'l0rinc's LLMs recently found changing the passphrase can leave the original that encryption key record in free pages. We should want to ensure that those records are also deleted... Note that this behavior appears to be present since wallet encryption was initially introduced in #352.'",
  "PR description: 'Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, Arch, and NixOS all set SQLite's compile time option to default secure_delete to enabled... This suggests to me that the performance penalty is not actually that bad.'"
 ],

<category name="build" title="Build and CI">
## Covers

How the project is built, tested, and released: the CMake build system,
the depends system and its packages, Guix reproducible builds, CI
configuration and scripts, compiler and platform support, and the
tooling under contrib used for releases and development. Platform
labels (Windows, macOS) point here when the change is about building or
running on that platform rather than about a feature. The Build system
label is a strong prior.

Not build: source changes that happen to fix a compiler warning as a
side effect (they belong to their area).

## What matters here

Release integrity first: reproducibility of Guix builds, correctness of
dependency pinning and verification, and anything that could ship a
wrong binary. Then supported-platform breakage: a platform that fails
to build or run blocks users on it. Then CI reliability: flaky or
misleading jobs waste every contributor's time and hide real failures.
Then dependency transitions with deadlines (compiler or library minimum
versions, deprecations upstream). Then build time and contributor
friction.

Cosmetic CMake cleanups rank low unless they remove a recurring
breakage.

<category name="wallet" title="Wallet">
## Covers

The bitcoind wallet: key and descriptor management, transaction creation
and coin selection, PSBT handling, wallet database (SQLite, and the
legacy BDB migration path), backup and recovery, rescanning, wallet RPCs,
and wallet-facing pieces of the GUI. Fee estimation is wallet when the
change is about how the wallet uses it.

Borderline: a descriptor or PSBT change that affects only `bitcoin-tx` or
RPC without wallet code is rpc, not wallet. An `interfaces::Wallet`
change is both wallet and ipc.

## What matters here

Fund safety first: anything that could lose keys, double-spend
unintentionally, create an unspendable output, or corrupt the wallet
database. Then backup, recovery, and migration correctness, including the
legacy-to-descriptor migration path that every remaining legacy user
must cross. Then privacy of transaction creation (address reuse, change
detection, fingerprinting). Then user-visible reliability: hangs, slow
rescans, confusing failures, wrong balances. Then features users have
asked for, with evidence they have asked.

The rubric does not ask whether Bitcoin Core should have a wallet. It
asks, given that it does, what a wallet user needs most.
